unit.title: Designing and governing agents at school

lesson.title: Design an agent for a school job
lesson.subtitle: Start from the job, give the fewest tools, split it into roles

video.title: Design an agent for a school job
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A list: Answer parents; Check attendance; Every tool?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Our head teacher wants an agent for the school office. It should answer parents, check attendance and send the weekly news. Someone said: give it every tool, so it never gets stuck. Good design?

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Design an agent for a school job
scenes.narration: Today: designing an agent for a school job, with the fewest tools and clear roles.

scenes.visual: A list: The job, in one sentence; Who uses it; What a mistake costs.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Good design starts from the job, not the tools. Who will use it, and what should it do? And what would a mistake cost: a wrong reminder, or a wrong message to a parent?

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Then give it only the tools that job needs. An agent acts only through its tools, so every extra tool is another way to go wrong. A homework helper needs the timetable and the library, nothing more.

scenes.visual: A list: The fewest tools; The least data; A misread does less harm; Like staff accounts.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: This is called least privilege: the fewest tools and the least data the job needs. If the agent misreads a request, it can’t do much harm. It’s the rule we already use for staff accounts.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Next, split the work into roles. The planner, the model, proposes each tool call. A checker, a few strict rules in code, reviews it before it runs. The app runs it, and a person approves any action.

scenes.visual: A list: The tool is on; Each detail has the right shape; Names and numbers from your words; No earlier step failed; A person said yes.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The team lab’s checker has five rules. The tool is on. Each detail has the right shape. Every name and number came from your words or a result. No earlier step failed. And a person said yes to any action.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! An office agent only answers parents’ questions about homework. Which tools should it get?

scenes.visual: A list: Timetable: yes; Library: yes; Messages, attendance: no; A new tool later? With approval.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The timetable and the library. Nothing in that job sends messages or reads attendance. If parents later want replies by message, add that tool then, with a person approving each one.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: PERMS = { …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Write the permissions down as a table, one line per tool. Here, the weather and the timetable run freely, while reminders and messages wait for a yes. Any tool that isn’t in the table is off.

scenes.visual: A list: Weather: it passes; 9Z written as 9C; The checker stops it; Checker off: try again.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: a planner and a checker
scenes.narration: In the app, send the weather request: the checker passes it. Then ask what nine Z has tomorrow: Darsi Tiny writes nine C, and the checker stops it. Turn the checker off and try again.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Who should approve the weekly news before the agent sends it to parents?

scenes.visual: Summary points: Start from the job; Fewest tools, in a table; Roles; a person approves.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: Start from the job · Fewest tools, in a table · Roles; a person approves
scenes.narration: A named person at school, every time. Remember: start from the job and what a mistake costs. Give the fewest tools, in a permissions table. Split the work into roles, and a person approves actions.

scenes.visual: A list: A design sprint in groups; One page: job, tools, approvals; How will we know it works?; Swap: hunt for an extra tool.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: run a design sprint. Groups pick a school job and write a one-page design: the job, the tools, who approves, and how we’ll know it works. Then they swap and hunt for an extra tool.

checkpoints.prompt: An office agent only answers parents’ questions about homework. Which tools should it get?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the job needs the timetable and the library, nothing more. Fewer tools mean fewer ways to go wrong.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — give only the tools the job needs. Messages and attendance aren’t part of answering homework questions.

checkpoints.prompt: Who should approve the weekly news before the agent sends it to parents?

options.text: The agent itself, if it’s confident

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a message to every parent is an action. A named person reads it and says yes, and the school knows who is responsible.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the agent’s confidence isn’t a check, and news to every parent is an action. A named person approves it.
